# Do men or women have more brothers?

## 0. The answer

Under the four assumptions as stated — in particular under assumption 4, that within a family
the sex of each member is independent of the sexes of the other members — the answer is:

> **Neither. The number of brothers of a randomly chosen woman and the number of brothers of a
> randomly chosen man have exactly the same distribution** (hence the same expectation),
> *whatever* the distribution of family sizes, and indeed whatever the common sex ratio $p$.

The common expectation is $p\,\bar\nu$, where $\bar\nu$ is the mean number of siblings of a
uniformly chosen individual; for $p=\frac12$ it is $\bar\nu/2$.

The one-line refutation of the "two girls and one boy" argument is:

> The family of a randomly chosen man contains on average **exactly one more man** than the
> family of a randomly chosen woman — namely, *himself*. He is not his own brother, and the
> two "exactly one"s cancel identically.

Sections 1–3 set up the model and prove this; Section 4 gives the exact bookkeeping that
refutes the within-family argument; Section 5 shows by counterexample that assumption 4 (and a
homogeneity assumption hidden in assumption 1) is genuinely load-bearing, so no softer argument
could give the answer; Section 6 analyses the variant model in which the number of men is
*exactly* half of the population — which strictly speaking contradicts assumption 4 — and there
the questioner's intuition is vindicated, but only by a margin $\bar\nu/(M-1)$ that vanishes as
the population size $M$ grows.

---

## 1. The model

**Population and families.** Let the population be a finite set $[M]=\{1,\dots ,M\}$ of
individuals, partitioned into nonempty families $C_1,\dots ,C_F$ with $|C_j|=n_j\ge 1$ and
$\sum_{j=1}^{F}n_j=M$. Write $f(i)$ for the index of the family containing $i$, and
$n(i):=n_{f(i)}$ for the size of $i$'s family. The partition is arbitrary and **fixed**
(deterministic); no assumption whatsoever is made about the multiset of sizes $\{n_j\}$ — this
is assumption 3 ("deliberately not specified") taken at face value. Everything below also
holds if the partition is itself random, provided it is independent of the sexes: simply
condition on it, note that the conclusions do not depend on it, and average.

**Sexes.** Let $S_1,\dots ,S_M$ take values in $\{\mathrm m,\mathrm f\}$ and assume:

* **(H1) Homogeneity.** There is a single $p\in(0,1)$ with $\mathbb P(S_i=\mathrm m)=p$ for
  every $i$. This is assumption 1, read as "a fraction $p=\frac12$ of the population is male on
  average"; we keep $p$ general, to exhibit that the conclusion depends on it not at all.
  Section 6 treats the alternative, literal reading of assumption 1.
* **(H2) Within-family independence.** For every $i$, the variable $S_i$ is independent of the
  vector $(S_k)_{k\in C_{f(i)}\setminus\{i\}}$. This is assumption 4, verbatim.
* **(H3)** Sexes in different families are independent.

(H3) is convenient but, as the proof will show, never used for the main theorem; it is needed
only for the law-of-large-numbers statement of Section 3.

The following elementary lemma says that (H2), though phrased as a list of "one against the
rest" statements, already delivers full mutual independence inside each family. It is worth
recording because the binomial computations below use mutual independence.

> **Lemma 0.** Let $X_1,\dots ,X_n$ be random variables with values in a finite set such that
> for every $i$, $X_i$ is independent of $(X_k)_{k\ne i}$. Then $X_1,\dots ,X_n$ are mutually
> independent.

*Proof.* Induction on $n$; the cases $n\le 2$ are immediate. Let $n\ge 3$ and abbreviate
$P(x_1,\dots ,x_n)=\mathbb P(X_1=x_1,\dots ,X_n=x_n)$. The hypothesis for $i=1$ gives
$$P(x_1,\dots ,x_n)=\mathbb P(X_1=x_1)\,P_{2:n}(x_2,\dots ,x_n),\tag{1}$$
where $P_{2:n}$ is the joint law of $(X_2,\dots ,X_n)$. Fix $i\ge 2$ and sum the hypothesis for
that $i$, namely $P(x_1,\dots ,x_n)=\mathbb P(X_i=x_i)\,\mathbb P\bigl((X_k)_{k\ne i}=(x_k)_{k\ne i}\bigr)$,
over all values of $x_1$: the left side becomes $P_{2:n}(x_2,\dots ,x_n)$ and the right side
becomes $\mathbb P(X_i=x_i)\,\mathbb P\bigl((X_k)_{k\in\{2,\dots ,n\}\setminus\{i\}}=(x_k)_k\bigr)$.
Hence inside the family $(X_2,\dots ,X_n)$ each variable is again independent of the others, so
by the inductive hypothesis $P_{2:n}=\prod_{k=2}^{n}\mathbb P(X_k=\cdot)$; substituting into (1)
finishes the induction. $\blacksquare$

By (H1), (H2) and Lemma 0, **the sexes inside any one family are i.i.d. Bernoulli($p$)**; with
(H3) all $M$ sexes are i.i.d.

**Brothers.** For $i\in[M]$ put
$$B_i\;:=\;\#\{k\in C_{f(i)}:k\ne i,\ S_k=\mathrm m\}\;=\!\!\sum_{k\in C_{f(i)}\setminus\{i\}}\!\!\mathbf 1\{S_k=\mathrm m\},$$
the number of brothers of $i$ (male siblings, oneself excluded — the point the questioner
rightly insists on). Note that $B_i$ is a function of $(S_k)_{k\ne i}$ alone: **$B_i$ does not
involve $S_i$.** This triviality is the entire content of the theorem below; the work consists
in checking that no other channel lets $S_I$ influence $B_I$.

**Sampling an individual.** Let $I$ be a random index in $[M]$, **independent of
$(S_1,\dots ,S_M)$**, with arbitrary law $\mathbb P(I=i)=w_i\ge0$, $\sum_i w_i=1$. The two
random variables in the question are then "$B_I$ given $S_I=\mathrm f$" and "$B_I$ given
$S_I=\mathrm m$". The default choice is $w_i\equiv 1/M$ ("pick a person uniformly at random"),
which automatically implements the size-biasing by which large families contribute more
individuals; the choice $w_i=\frac{1}{F\,n(i)}$ ("pick a family uniformly, then one of its
members uniformly") is also allowed, as is any other weighting. The theorem is indifferent to
which is used, which disposes in advance of the objection that the answer is an artefact of a
sampling convention.

Since $I\perp(S_1,\dots,S_M)$ and by (H1), $\mathbb P(S_I=\mathrm m)=\sum_i w_i\,\mathbb P(S_i=\mathrm m)=p\in(0,1)$
and $\mathbb P(S_I=\mathrm f)=1-p>0$, so both conditionings are legitimate.

---

## 2. The theorem

Define
$$\bar\nu\;:=\;\sum_{i\in[M]}w_i\bigl(n(i)-1\bigr),$$
the expected number of siblings of the sampled individual. For uniform sampling
$w_i\equiv1/M$ this is $\bar\nu=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^{F}n_j(n_j-1)$, the size-biased mean sibship
size.

> **Theorem 1.** Assume (H1), (H2) and $I\perp (S_1,\dots ,S_M)$. Then for every integer
> $k\ge0$,
> $$\mathbb P\bigl(B_I=k\mid S_I=\mathrm f\bigr)=\mathbb P\bigl(B_I=k\mid S_I=\mathrm m\bigr)
> =\sum_{i\in[M]}w_i\binom{n(i)-1}{k}p^{k}(1-p)^{\,n(i)-1-k}.$$
> In particular the two conditional expectations exist and are equal:
> $$\mathbb E\bigl[B_I\mid S_I=\mathrm f\bigr]=\mathbb E\bigl[B_I\mid S_I=\mathrm m\bigr]=p\,\bar\nu .$$

*Proof.* Fix $i\in[M]$ and $s\in\{\mathrm m,\mathrm f\}$.

*Step 1: $B_i\perp S_i$.* The variable $B_i$ is a function of $(S_k)_{k\in C_{f(i)}\setminus\{i\}}$,
and by (H2) that vector is independent of $S_i$. Hence
$\mathbb P(B_i=k,\,S_i=s)=\mathbb P(B_i=k)\,\mathbb P(S_i=s)$ for all $k,s$.

*Step 2: the law of $B_i$.* By (H1), (H2) and Lemma 0 the sexes within $C_{f(i)}$ are i.i.d.
Bernoulli($p$), so $B_i$ is a sum of $n(i)-1$ i.i.d. Bernoulli($p$) indicators:
$B_i\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n(i)-1,p)$, with $\mathbb E B_i=(n(i)-1)p$. (When $n(i)=1$ this reads
$B_i\equiv 0$, correctly.)

*Step 3: conditioning on sex does not bias the sample.* Because $I$ is independent of the whole
sex vector, and by (H1) $\mathbb P(S_i=s)=\mathbb P(S_1=s)$ for all $i$,
$$\mathbb P(I=i\mid S_I=s)=\frac{\mathbb P(I=i)\,\mathbb P(S_i=s)}{\mathbb P(S_I=s)}
=\frac{w_i\,\mathbb P(S_1=s)}{\mathbb P(S_1=s)}=w_i .$$
So, given the sampled individual's sex, their identity — and hence their family size — is still
distributed as $w$. (This is the step where homogeneity (H1) is used, and where it can fail: see
Section 5.)

*Step 4: combine.* Using $I\perp(S_k)_k$, then Step 1, then (H1):
$$\mathbb P\bigl(B_I=k,\ S_I=s\bigr)=\sum_i w_i\,\mathbb P(B_i=k,\ S_i=s)
=\Bigl(\sum_i w_i\,\mathbb P(B_i=k)\Bigr)\mathbb P(S_1=s),$$
while $\mathbb P(S_I=s)=\mathbb P(S_1=s)>0$. Dividing,
$$\mathbb P\bigl(B_I=k\mid S_I=s\bigr)=\sum_i w_i\,\mathbb P(B_i=k)
=\sum_i w_i\binom{n(i)-1}{k}p^{k}(1-p)^{n(i)-1-k},$$
which does not depend on $s$: the conditional law is, for either sex, the $w$-mixture of the
laws $\mathrm{Bin}(n(i)-1,p)$. Since $0\le B_I\le\max_j n_j<\infty$, expectations exist, and
summing $k\,\mathbb P(B_I=k\mid S_I=s)$ over $k$ gives
$\sum_i w_i\,\mathbb E B_i=\sum_i w_i (n(i)-1)p=p\bar\nu$ for both $s$. $\blacksquare$

Three comments.

* The proof used (H1), (H2) and the independence of the sampling from the sexes, and nothing
  else. Assumptions 2 and 3 played no role beyond fixing notation, and (H3) was not used. In
  particular **the conclusion is completely insensitive to the (deliberately unspecified)
  family-size distribution and to the sex ratio $p$**. So the answer to "even in the absence of
  any information about point 3, what can one say?" is the strongest possible one: not merely a
  bound relating the two expectations, but the statement that the two conditional
  *distributions* coincide, always and exactly.
* The same argument with $\mathrm m$ replaced by $\mathrm f$ in the definition of $B_i$ shows
  that men and women also have identically distributed numbers of *sisters*, namely the
  $w$-mixture of $\mathrm{Bin}(n(i)-1,1-p)$. For $p=\frac12$: everybody, of either sex, has on
  average $\bar\nu/2$ brothers and $\bar\nu/2$ sisters.
* Nothing in the argument requires "large numbers"; the identity is exact in every finite
  population, for every $M\ge1$.

---

## 3. The empirical ("go out and count") version

Theorem 1 concerns a randomly sampled individual. One might instead ask about the *realised*
averages in one large population. Write
$$b_j:=\#\{i\in C_j:S_i=\mathrm m\},\qquad g_j:=n_j-b_j$$
for the numbers of men and women in family $j$. Each of the $g_j$ women of family $j$ has
exactly $b_j$ brothers and each of its $b_j$ men has exactly $b_j-1$ — this is precisely where
the "in any single family the girls have more brothers" intuition lives — so the realised
averages are
$$A_{\mathrm f}:=\frac{\sum_{j}g_jb_j}{\sum_j g_j},\qquad
A_{\mathrm m}:=\frac{\sum_{j}b_j(b_j-1)}{\sum_j b_j}.$$

First, a remark that legitimises computing such ratios through expectations.

> **Lemma 2.** Assume only that $I\sim\mathrm{Unif}[M]$ is independent of $(S_1,\dots ,S_M)$ and
> that $\mathbb P(S_I=s)>0$. (Neither (H1) nor (H2) is needed; this will matter in Section 5.)
> Let $\varphi$ assign to each individual $i$ a number $\varphi_i$ determined by the sexes
> (e.g. $\varphi_i=B_i$, or $\varphi_i=b_{f(i)}$). Then
> $$\mathbb E[\varphi_I\mid S_I=s]=\frac{\mathbb E\bigl[\sum_i\varphi_i\mathbf 1\{S_i=s\}\bigr]}{\mathbb E\bigl[\#\{i:S_i=s\}\bigr]}.$$
> In particular
> $\mathbb E[B_I\mid S_I=\mathrm f]=\dfrac{\mathbb E[\sum_j g_jb_j]}{\mathbb E[\sum_j g_j]}$ and
> $\mathbb E[B_I\mid S_I=\mathrm m]=\dfrac{\mathbb E[\sum_j b_j(b_j-1)]}{\mathbb E[\sum_j b_j]}$:
> the conditional expectations are exactly the ratios of expectations that a bookkeeper would
> write down.

*Proof.* By independence of $I$ from the sexes,
$\mathbb E[\varphi_I\mathbf 1\{S_I=s\}]=\frac1M\mathbb E\bigl[\sum_i\varphi_i\mathbf 1\{S_i=s\}\bigr]$
and $\mathbb P(S_I=s)=\frac1M\mathbb E\bigl[\#\{i:S_i=s\}\bigr]>0$; divide. For the special
cases use the family-wise identities, valid for every fixed sex assignment,
$$\sum_{i\in C_j}B_i\mathbf 1\{S_i=\mathrm f\}=g_jb_j,\qquad
\sum_{i\in C_j}B_i\mathbf 1\{S_i=\mathrm m\}=b_j(b_j-1). \qquad\blacksquare$$

Now the law of large numbers. Let the families be indexed by $j=1,2,\dots$, let their sizes
$N_1,N_2,\dots$ be i.i.d. with $N_j\ge1$ and $\mathbb E[N_1^{2}]<\infty$, and, given the sizes,
let all individuals' sexes be i.i.d. Bernoulli($p$) (i.e. (H1)–(H3)). Let
$A^{(F)}_{\mathrm f},A^{(F)}_{\mathrm m}$ denote the above ratios computed from the first $F$
families.

> **Corollary 3.** Almost surely, $A^{(F)}_{\mathrm f}$ and $A^{(F)}_{\mathrm m}$ are eventually
> well defined and
> $$\lim_{F\to\infty}A^{(F)}_{\mathrm f}=\lim_{F\to\infty}A^{(F)}_{\mathrm m}
> =p\,\frac{\mathbb E[N_1(N_1-1)]}{\mathbb E[N_1]} .$$

*Proof.* The pairs $(b_j,g_j)$, $j\ge1$, are i.i.d., with $b_j\mid N_j\sim\mathrm{Bin}(N_j,p)$.
From the binomial moments $\mathbb E[b\mid N]=Np$, $\mathbb E[b(b-1)\mid N]=N(N-1)p^{2}$ and
$$\mathbb E[b(N-b)\mid N]=N\cdot Np-\bigl(N(N-1)p^{2}+Np\bigr)=N(N-1)p(1-p),$$
we get, all quantities finite because $\mathbb E[N_1^2]<\infty$,
$$\mathbb E[b_1]=p\,\mathbb E N_1,\quad \mathbb E[g_1]=(1-p)\mathbb E N_1,\quad
\mathbb E[b_1(b_1-1)]=p^{2}\mathbb E[N_1(N_1-1)],\quad \mathbb E[g_1b_1]=p(1-p)\mathbb E[N_1(N_1-1)].$$
By the strong law of large numbers, each of the four averages $\frac1F\sum_{j\le F}(\cdot)$
converges a.s. to the corresponding expectation. The two denominators have strictly positive
limits $p\,\mathbb E N_1>0$ and $(1-p)\mathbb E N_1>0$, so a.s. $\sum_{j\le F}b_j$ and
$\sum_{j\le F}g_j$ are eventually positive (the ratios are eventually defined), and
$$A^{(F)}_{\mathrm f}\longrightarrow\frac{p(1-p)\mathbb E[N_1(N_1-1)]}{(1-p)\mathbb E N_1}
=p\frac{\mathbb E[N_1(N_1-1)]}{\mathbb E N_1},\qquad
A^{(F)}_{\mathrm m}\longrightarrow\frac{p^{2}\mathbb E[N_1(N_1-1)]}{p\,\mathbb E N_1}
=p\frac{\mathbb E[N_1(N_1-1)]}{\mathbb E N_1}.\ \blacksquare$$

So the equality is not an artefact of the expectation operator either: if one really went out and
counted, the average number of brothers per woman and the average per man would converge to the
same number, $p\cdot$(size-biased mean sibship size).

---

## 4. Direct refutation of the within-family argument

The argument to be refuted runs:

> In any single family — say, two girls and one boy — the girls have at least as many brothers
> as the boys do, and usually strictly more (here $1$ versus $0$). So on average women must come
> out ahead.

The premise is **true**, in every family at once:

> **Fact.** In a family with $b$ men and $g$ women, each woman has exactly $b$ brothers and each
> man exactly $b-1$; so each woman has exactly **one more** brother than each man of the same
> family.

The inference nevertheless fails, and here is exactly where. An average over women is not an
average over families: it is an average over *women*, and different families supply different
numbers of women — and, crucially, the number of women a family supplies is correlated with the
number of brothers available in it. Throughout this section let
$$A_{\mathrm m}:=\mathbb E[B_I\mid S_I=\mathrm m],\qquad A_{\mathrm f}:=\mathbb E[B_I\mid S_I=\mathrm f]$$
(uniform sampling); by Lemma 2 these are the ratios of expectations displayed below, and by
Corollary 3 they are also the almost-sure limits of the realised averages of Section 3, so no
ambiguity arises from re-using the letters. By Lemma 2 and the family-wise identities in its
proof,
$$A_{\mathrm m}=\frac{\sum_j\mathbb E[b_j(b_j-1)]}{\sum_j\mathbb E[b_j]}
=\underbrace{\frac{\sum_j\mathbb E[b_j^{2}]}{\sum_j\mathbb E[b_j]}}_{\textstyle =: \mathcal B}-1,
\qquad
A_{\mathrm f}=\underbrace{\frac{\sum_j\mathbb E[g_jb_j]}{\sum_j\mathbb E[g_j]}}_{\textstyle =: \mathcal G}.$$
By Lemma 2 applied to $\varphi_i=b_{f(i)}$ (the number of men in $i$'s family),
$$\mathcal B=\mathbb E\bigl[\#\text{men in }C_{f(I)}\ \big|\ S_I=\mathrm m\bigr],\qquad
\mathcal G=\mathbb E\bigl[\#\text{men in }C_{f(I)}\ \big|\ S_I=\mathrm f\bigr],$$
i.e. $\mathcal B$ is the expected number of men in the family of a randomly chosen **man** and
$\mathcal G$ the expected number of men in the family of a randomly chosen **woman**. The
informal argument sees the $-1$ in $A_{\mathrm m}=\mathcal B-1$ ("no man is his own brother") but
overlooks that $\mathcal B\ne\mathcal G$: men are over-represented in man-rich families, because
such families contain more men to be sampled. (For a single family size $n$ this is literal
size-biasing: the sampled man's family has $b$ men with probability proportional to
$b\,\mathbb P(b)$, the sampled woman's with probability proportional to $(n-b)\mathbb P(b)$; the
likelihood ratio $b/(n-b)$ is increasing in $b$, so the first law strictly dominates the second
stochastically.) The two effects cancel, and they cancel exactly:

> **Proposition 4.** Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1 with uniform sampling,
> $$\mathcal B-\mathcal G=1,\qquad\text{hence}\qquad A_{\mathrm m}=\mathcal B-1=\mathcal G=A_{\mathrm f}=p\,\bar\nu .$$

*Proof.* Two proofs, one computational and one conceptual.

*(a) Computation.* Within family $j$ the sexes are i.i.d. Bernoulli($p$), so
$b_j\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n_j,p)$ and
$$\mathbb E[b_j]=n_jp,\quad \mathbb E[g_j]=n_j(1-p),\quad
\mathbb E[b_j^{2}]=n_jp(1-p)+n_j^{2}p^{2},\quad \mathbb E[g_jb_j]=n_j(n_j-1)p(1-p),$$
the last as computed in Corollary 3. Writing $\Sigma_1:=\sum_jn_j=M$ and
$\Sigma_2:=\sum_jn_j^{2}$,
$$\mathcal B=\frac{p(1-p)\Sigma_1+p^{2}\Sigma_2}{p\,\Sigma_1}=(1-p)+p\frac{\Sigma_2}{\Sigma_1},
\qquad
\mathcal G=\frac{p(1-p)(\Sigma_2-\Sigma_1)}{(1-p)\Sigma_1}=p\frac{\Sigma_2}{\Sigma_1}-p,$$
whence $\mathcal B-\mathcal G=(1-p)+p=1$. Also $\mathcal G=p\frac{\Sigma_2-\Sigma_1}{\Sigma_1}
=p\cdot\frac1M\sum_jn_j(n_j-1)=p\bar\nu$, and $A_{\mathrm m}=\mathcal B-1=\mathcal G=A_{\mathrm f}$.

*(b) Conceptual.* By Step 3 of Theorem 1, conditioning on the sampled individual's sex does not
change the distribution of their identity, hence not that of their family size $n(I)$; and by
Step 1 it does not change the law of the other members' sexes. Therefore the family of a randomly
chosen man consists of *himself*, a man, together with $\mathrm{Bin}(n(I)-1,p)$ further men,
giving $\mathcal B=1+\mathbb E[(n(I)-1)]p=1+p\bar\nu$; while the family of a randomly chosen woman
consists of herself, a woman, together with $\mathrm{Bin}(n(I)-1,p)$ men, giving
$\mathcal G=p\bar\nu$. Subtract. $\blacksquare$

So the refutation, in one sentence: **a man's family contains on average exactly one more man
than a woman's family does — namely himself — and he is precisely the one man of his family who
is not his own brother.** Deduct him and the two counts of *brothers* agree; and by Theorem 1
they agree not just on average but in distribution, both being the mixture of
$\mathrm{Bin}(n(i)-1,p)$.

Put still differently: the intuitive argument tacitly compares a man and a woman **drawn from
the same family**, i.e. it conditions on the family composition $(b,g)$, and that conditional
comparison is entirely correct, giving the man a deficit of exactly $1$. But conditioning on the
composition is not free: composition governs how many individuals of each sex are available to be
sampled. Unconditionally, a man's own sex is evidence that his family holds one extra man
(himself), worth exactly $+1$. The fallacy is the standard inspection-paradox error of averaging
a within-stratum contrast without re-weighting the strata by their differing sampling
probabilities.

A concrete illustration, $n=3$, $p=\frac12$, per $8$ families of three children:

| composition $(b,g)$ | #families | brothers per man | brothers per woman | men | women | brothers accruing to men | brothers accruing to women |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $(3,0)$ | 1 | 2 | — | 3 | 0 | 6 | 0 |
| $(2,1)$ | 3 | 1 | 2 | 6 | 3 | 6 | 6 |
| $(1,2)$ | 3 | 0 | 1 | 3 | 6 | 0 | 6 |
| $(0,3)$ | 1 | — | 0 | 0 | 3 | 0 | 0 |
| **total** | **8** | | | **12** | **12** | **12** | **12** |

In every row in which both sexes are present the women beat the men by exactly $1$, exactly as
the intuitive argument says. Yet the column totals agree: $12/12=1=(n-1)p$ for each sex. The
women's advantage in the two middle rows is exactly consumed by the top row, the all-boy family,
which contributes three men with two brothers apiece and no women at all — the row in which the
"girls have more brothers than boys" comparison has no girls to apply to. That is the
re-weighting the informal argument forgets.

---

## 5. Both hypotheses are essential: three counterexamples

The equality is not a formal triviality that would survive any reasonable modelling. It uses
(H2) — within-family independence — and (H1) — a common sex ratio for all individuals — in an
essential way. Each can fail while assumptions 1–3 hold, and then either sex can win.

**(i) Prescribed compositions; women win.** Take $2F$ families: $F$ consisting of $2$ girls and
$1$ boy, and $F$ consisting of $2$ boys and $1$ girl. The population is exactly half male
($3F$ of each). Women: $2F$ of them have $1$ brother and $F$ have $2$, so
$A_{\mathrm f}=\frac{2F+2F}{3F}=\frac43$. Men: $F$ have $0$ brothers and $2F$ have $1$, so
$A_{\mathrm m}=\frac{2F}{3F}=\frac23$. Women have twice as many brothers on average.

**(ii) Prescribed compositions; men win.** Take $F$ all-boy families of size $3$ and $F$
all-girl families of size $3$. Again exactly half the population is male. Every woman has $0$
brothers; every man has $2$. Men win outright.

Both examples respect assumptions 1, 2, 3 and violate (H2). Example (ii) also shows that the
premise "in any single family girls have at least as many brothers as boys", though true, can be
wholly vacuous: in an all-boy family there is no girl to enjoy the advantage, and in an all-girl
family there is no brother to be had. Any valid argument must therefore control how the sexes are
spread across families — which is exactly what (H2) does and what the informal argument omits.

**(iii) Heterogeneous sex propensities; men win.** This one satisfies within-family independence
and so is the more instructive failure. Suppose family $j$ has its own propensity $p_j$, and
given the propensities all sexes are independent with $\mathbb P(S_i=\mathrm m)=p_{f(i)}$; then
(H2) holds verbatim (sexes within a family are independent), but (H1) fails, and Step 3 of
Theorem 1 breaks down: knowing that the sampled individual is male is now evidence that they come
from a boy-prone family, which is exactly the kind of family in which brothers are plentiful.
Concretely, take $F$ families of size $2$ with $p_j=0.9$ and $F$ of size $2$ with $p_j=0.1$; the
population is half male on average ($2F$ expected men out of $4F$ individuals). Since $B_i$ is
still independent of $S_i$, Lemma 2 with $\varphi_i=B_i$ gives, for uniform sampling,
$$\mathbb E[B_I\mid S_I=\mathrm m]=\frac{\sum_i\mathbb E[B_i]\,p_{f(i)}}{\sum_i p_{f(i)}},\qquad
\mathbb E[B_I\mid S_I=\mathrm f]=\frac{\sum_i\mathbb E[B_i]\,(1-p_{f(i)})}{\sum_i(1-p_{f(i)})},$$
two *differently weighted* averages of the same numbers $\mathbb E[B_i]$ — and there is no reason
for them to agree. Here a member of a $0.9$-family has $\mathbb E B_i=0.9$ and is male with
probability $0.9$, a member of a $0.1$-family has $\mathbb E B_i=0.1$ and is male with
probability $0.1$, and the two kinds of individual are equinumerous, so
$$\mathbb E[B_I\mid S_I=\mathrm m]=\frac{0.9\cdot0.9+0.1\cdot0.1}{0.9+0.1}=0.82,\qquad
\mathbb E[B_I\mid S_I=\mathrm f]=\frac{0.9\cdot 0.1+0.1\cdot0.9}{0.1+0.9}=0.18 .$$
Men have more than four times as many brothers. So the "no man is his own brother" effect is not
merely cancellable — it can be swamped in either direction.

---

## 6. The other reading of "half are men": exactly $M/2$ men

Assumption 1 says half the individuals are men; assumption 4 says the sexes within a family are
independent. Taken literally *and* simultaneously, these are inconsistent: independent coin flips
produce exactly $M/2$ heads only with probability $\Theta(M^{-1/2})$, and conditioning on that
event destroys independence. Section 1 resolved the tension in the usual way, by reading
assumption 1 as $p=\frac12$. It is instructive to resolve it the other way, because then the
questioner's intuition *is* vindicated — but only at order $1/M$.

**Model B.** $M$ even; the set $A\subseteq[M]$ of men is uniformly distributed over all
$\binom{M}{M/2}$ subsets of size $M/2$; the family partition $C_1,\dots ,C_F$ is as in Section 1;
and $I\sim\mathrm{Unif}[M]$ is independent of $A$. The sexes are now exchangeable but *negatively*
correlated, so (H2) fails — slightly. Keep $\bar\nu=\frac1M\sum_jn_j(n_j-1)$.

> **Theorem 5.** In Model B,
> $$\mathbb E[B_I\mid S_I=\mathrm f]=\bar\nu\,\frac{M/2}{M-1},\qquad
> \mathbb E[B_I\mid S_I=\mathrm m]=\bar\nu\,\frac{M/2-1}{M-1},$$
> and therefore
> $$\mathbb E[B_I\mid S_I=\mathrm f]-\mathbb E[B_I\mid S_I=\mathrm m]=\frac{\bar\nu}{M-1}\;>\;0,$$
> the inequality being strict as soon as some family has $n_j\ge2$.

*Proof.* By exchangeability $\mathbb P(i\in A)=\frac12$ for every $i$, and $I\perp A$, so
$$\mathbb P(I=i\mid S_I=s)=\frac{(1/M)\cdot(1/2)}{1/2}=\frac1M$$
for either $s$: as in Model A, the sampled individual's identity (hence family size) is
independent of their sex. Next fix $i$. All $(M/2)$-subsets have the same probability
$\binom{M}{M/2}^{-1}$, so conditionally on $\{i\notin A\}$ the set $A$ is uniform over the
$(M/2)$-subsets of $[M]\setminus\{i\}$; hence for $k\ne i$,
$\mathbb P(k\in A\mid i\notin A)=\frac{\binom{M-2}{M/2-1}}{\binom{M-1}{M/2}}=\frac{M/2}{M-1}$, and
by linearity
$$\mathbb E[B_i\mid S_i=\mathrm f]=(n(i)-1)\frac{M/2}{M-1}.$$
Conditionally on $\{i\in A\}$, $A\setminus\{i\}$ is uniform over the $(M/2-1)$-subsets of
$[M]\setminus\{i\}$, so $\mathbb P(k\in A\mid i\in A)=\frac{M/2-1}{M-1}$ and
$\mathbb E[B_i\mid S_i=\mathrm m]=(n(i)-1)\frac{M/2-1}{M-1}$. Finally, using $I\perp A$ and
$\mathbb P(S_i=s)=\mathbb P(S_I=s)=\frac12$,
$$\mathbb E[B_I\mid S_I=s]=\frac{\mathbb E[B_I\mathbf 1\{S_I=s\}]}{\mathbb P(S_I=s)}
=\frac{\frac1M\sum_i\mathbb E[B_i\mathbf 1\{S_i=s\}]}{1/2}=\frac1M\sum_i\mathbb E[B_i\mid S_i=s],$$
and $\frac1M\sum_i(n(i)-1)=\frac1M\sum_jn_j(n_j-1)=\bar\nu$ gives the two displayed formulas.
Subtracting, the difference is $\bar\nu\frac{(M/2)-(M/2-1)}{M-1}=\frac{\bar\nu}{M-1}$, and
$\bar\nu>0$ precisely when some $n_j\ge2$. $\blacksquare$

So in a *strictly* balanced population women do have more brothers: the "no man is his own
brother" intuition is not empty after all. But the margin is
$$\frac{\bar\nu}{M-1}\;\le\;\frac{\max_jn_j-1}{M-1}\;\xrightarrow[M\to\infty]{}\;0,$$
of the order (average sibship size)/(population size) — about $10^{-10}$ of a brother per woman in
a world of $10^{10}$ people, against a typical $\bar\nu/2$ of order $1$. The mechanism is
transparent: learning that $I$ is male uses up one of the world's $M/2$ men, lowering the chance
that any given sibling is male from $\frac{M/2}{M-1}$ to $\frac{M/2-1}{M-1}$. In Model A the
supply of men is inexhaustible — each new sibling is an independent coin flip — the depletion
effect is absent, and the difference is exactly $0$. Notice also that this residual effect is
*global*, not familial: it has nothing to do with the within-family comparison of Section 4, and
it would be there even if every family had exactly two members.

---

## 7. Conclusion

* **Under the stated assumptions the two expectations are equal** — indeed the two conditional
  *distributions* are equal: a randomly chosen man and a randomly chosen woman both have a number
  of brothers distributed as the ($w$-mixture of) $\mathrm{Bin}(n(i)-1,p)$, with common mean
  $p\,\bar\nu$; for $p=\frac12$, half the mean sibship size. This holds for every family-size
  distribution, every sex ratio and every sampling weighting, so the deliberate
  non-specification of point 3 costs nothing: no information about family sizes is needed, and
  none would change the answer.
* **The "two girls and one boy" argument is correct family by family but commits an
  inspection-paradox error when aggregating**: averaging over women weights families by their
  number of women, averaging over men weights them by their number of men. Quantitatively, the
  family of a random man contains on average exactly one more man than that of a random woman —
  himself — which exactly compensates the fact that he is not his own brother (Proposition 4).
  The $n=3$ table exhibits the cancellation line by line.
* **The hypotheses are doing real work**: with prescribed family compositions, or with
  family-specific sex propensities, and an exactly balanced population, either sex can have
  strictly more brothers on average, by an arbitrary margin (Section 5).
* **If one insists that exactly half the population be male** (abandoning strict independence),
  women do have more brothers — by exactly $\bar\nu/(M-1)$, a real but vanishing effect
  (Theorem 5). This, and only this, is the grain of truth in "no man can be his own brother".
